title: AI in Education: Teaching and Learning with AI
subtitle: Use a chat assistant to plan lessons, make materials, give feedback and tutor, while redesigning assessment, protecting learners' privacy and teaching students to use AI well.
outcomes: Plan lessons and create differentiated materials with an AI assistant, and check them before they reach learners
Draft feedback and build AI tutors that guide learners to think rather than giving them answers
Redesign assessments for a world with AI, with clear rules on permitted use and fair responses to suspected misuse
Use AI to make learning more accessible and inclusive, within privacy law and school policy
Teach learners how AI works, where it fails and how to use and acknowledge it honestly
prerequisites: None: this course is for teachers, lecturers, tutors and teaching assistants at any level. You need access to a chat assistant such as Claude, under a plan your school allows. Have a topic you teach in mind for the labs, and your school's AI or data-protection policy if it has one.
description: Chat assistants can save teachers hours of planning and preparation, and can help every learner get explanations, practice and feedback. They can also make mistakes, invite shortcuts and put learners' data at risk. This course shows how to get the benefits while keeping your professional judgement in charge. You'll plan lessons and make differentiated materials with an assistant, and check them for accuracy, level and bias. You'll draft feedback against your success criteria and build a Socratic tutor that helps learners think rather than handing them answers, testing it the way learners will use it. You'll redesign assessment for a world where AI can write a passable essay: assessing process, setting clear rules on permitted use, and responding fairly when misuse is suspected, without relying on unreliable AI detectors. Finally, you'll make materials more accessible, follow privacy law and school policy, and teach learners how AI works and how to use it honestly. Each lab produces something you can use in your own teaching, and the course ends with an AI-ready unit of work.

modules.title: Lesson planning and materials
modules.summary: Plan lessons with an assistant, create worksheets, quizzes and texts at different levels, and check everything before it reaches learners.

lessons.title: Planning lessons with an AI assistant
objectives: Give an assistant the context it needs to draft a useful lesson plan
Adapt an AI-drafted plan with professional judgement
key_points: A good planning prompt states the learners' age or grade, the curriculum objective, what they already know, the lesson length, the resources available and any learners who need extra support or challenge.
Ask for a plan with timings: a starter, explanation with worked examples, practice, a check for understanding and a plenary, then adjust it to your class.
Assistants are good at generating options, such as several ways to introduce a topic or examples from everyday life, which you choose from and adapt.
Ask for local, relevant contexts, such as prices in your currency or places your learners know, because default examples often assume one country's culture.
The teacher stays the professional: an AI plan doesn't know your learners, your curriculum's exact wording or what happened in last week's lesson.

walkthrough.title: Draft a lesson plan from the right context

steps.do: Give the assistant the context, then ask for the plan.
steps.code:
Help me plan a lesson.
Learners: 28 learners aged 10 to 11. Most can find equivalent fractions; a few still find it hard.
Objective: add fractions with different denominators, such as 1/2 + 1/3.
Length: 45 minutes. Resources: whiteboard and paper fraction strips; no devices for learners.
Give me a plan with timings: a starter, a short explanation with two worked examples, practice at two levels, a quick check for understanding and a plenary. Use everyday examples from [your country].
steps.see: A timed plan with worked examples, such as 1/2 + 1/3 = 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.

steps.do: Check each worked example yourself before going further.
Ask for alternatives for the part you're least happy with.
steps.code: Give me three different starter activities for this lesson, each under 5 minutes, using the fraction strips.

steps.do: Edit the plan for your class: the names of groups, the learners who need support, and what you know about their misconceptions.

lessons.title: Creating materials and resources
objectives: Create worksheets, examples and quizzes with an assistant
Produce versions of a resource for different levels
key_points: Assistants can draft worksheets, worked examples, quiz questions with answer keys, glossaries, reading passages and discussion prompts in minutes.
Differentiation is quicker: ask for the same task at three levels of difficulty, or for a text rewritten at a lower reading level with the key terms kept and explained.
Multiple-choice questions work better when the wrong options reflect common misconceptions, so ask the assistant to base them on the mistakes learners really make.
Ask for answer keys with full working, so you can check the reasoning and not only the final answers.
Check copyright and your school's rules before uploading textbook pages or other published material to an AI tool, and before sharing AI-made resources widely.

walkthrough.title: Make one text at three reading levels

steps.do: Paste a short text you use, with instructions kept apart from it.
steps.code:
Rewrite the text below at three levels for learners aged 12 to 13: (1) as written, (2) simpler sentences with the same key terms, (3) simplest, with the key terms in bold and a short glossary at the end. Keep every fact the same.

Text:
"""
[paste your text]
"""

steps.do: Ask for questions that work with all three versions.
steps.code: Write 5 questions that learners reading any of the three versions can answer, with an answer key.

steps.do: Read all three versions against the original, checking that no fact has changed or been lost.

lessons.title: Checking AI-made materials
objectives: Check AI-made materials for accuracy, bias and suitability
Use a checklist before materials reach learners
key_points: AI-made materials can contain factual errors, wrong answers in answer keys, mistakes in maths working and made-up references, so check every item before learners see it.
Work through each question yourself, as a learner would, which catches ambiguous wording and questions with more than one right answer.
Check for bias and stereotypes in names, roles and examples, such as always making the engineer a man, and for content unsuitable for your learners' age.
Check alignment: does each activity really practise the lesson's objective, at the level your curriculum expects?
Keep a short checklist (accuracy, answers, level, bias, alignment and age) and use it every time, because errors are easy to miss in fluent, well-formatted text.

lab.title: Plan a lesson and check its materials
lab.goal: Plan a lesson with an assistant, create a worksheet at two levels with an answer key, check every item, and adapt the plan for a real class.
setup: A chat assistant such as Claude
A topic you teach, or the sample: adding fractions with different denominators, for learners aged 10 to 11, in a 45-minute lesson

steps.do: Write a planning prompt giving the learners' age, the objective, their prior knowledge, the lesson length, the resources and any learners who need support. Copy the plan you get under the heading Lesson plan.
Ask for a worksheet of eight questions at two levels, with an answer key showing full working.
Work every question yourself. Under the heading Corrections, list each error you found and how you fixed it, or write that you found none and how you checked.
Under the heading Checklist, note your verdict on accuracy, answers, level, bias, alignment and age-suitability.
Under the heading Changes for my class, make and explain at least two changes based on what you know about your learners.

checks.text: A plan with timings is included, made from a prompt with the learners' age, objective, prior knowledge, length and resources.
A worksheet at two levels has an answer key with working.
Every answer was checked by working it, and any errors are corrected.
The checklist covers accuracy, answers, level, bias, alignment and age.
At least two changes are made for a real class, with reasons.

lab.submit: Paste your prompt, your Lesson plan, the worksheet and answer key, and your Corrections, Checklist and Changes for my class sections.
hints: Errors hide in answer keys: an assistant can set a right question and then give a wrong answer to it.
If the plan doesn't fit 45 minutes, ask the assistant to cut it to fit, then check what it dropped.

modules.title: Feedback and tutoring
modules.summary: Draft feedback learners can act on, build AI tutors that guide rather than tell, and test them the way learners will really use them.

lessons.title: AI-assisted feedback
objectives: Use an assistant to draft feedback against success criteria
Keep feedback personal, accurate and private
key_points: Effective feedback tells learners where they're going, how they're doing and what to do next, sometimes called feed up, feed back and feed forward.
An assistant can draft comments against your rubric or success criteria, suggest next steps and rephrase feedback for different reading levels, which you then check and personalise.
Remove names and identifying details before putting learners' work into an AI tool, and use only tools your school has approved for learners' data.
Don't let AI give final marks unchecked: models can be inconsistent, miss what's original in a piece of work and be swayed by length or polish.
Feedback works when learners act on it, so leave time for them to respond, redraft or try a similar task.

lessons.title: AI tutors that help learners think
objectives: Explain the difference between an AI tutor and an answer machine
Write instructions for a tutor that guides rather than tells
key_points: An assistant that simply gives answers lets learners skip the thinking that makes learning stick; a tutor asks questions, gives hints and leaves the work to the learner.
Socratic tutor instructions tell the assistant to ask one question at a time, never give the final answer, offer a small hint after a wrong attempt and ask learners to explain their reasoning.
Good tutor instructions name the topic and level, the misconceptions to watch for, and what to do if the learner asks for the answer or goes off topic.
Retrieval practice (recalling what was learned) and spaced practice (returning to it over days and weeks) are well-supported learning strategies that an assistant can provide through quizzes.
AI tutors still make mistakes, including marking a right answer wrong, so teach learners to question the tutor and to tell a teacher when something seems off.

steps.do: Start a new conversation with the tutor's role, rules and topic.
steps.code:
You are a maths tutor for learners aged 13 to 14 who are learning to solve equations like 2x + 3 = 11.
Rules:
- Never give the final answer, even if asked. Offer a hint or a question instead.
- Ask one question at a time and wait for the learner's reply.
- After a wrong step, give a small hint, not the correction.
- Ask the learner to explain why each step works.
- Watch for this common mistake: doing an operation to one side of the equation only.
- Keep to the topic, and use short, simple sentences.
Start by asking the learner what the first step could be.

steps.do: Reply as a learner who makes the common mistake.
steps.code: I take 3 away so it's 2x = 11, then x = 5.5
steps.see: A question that leads the learner to notice that 3 was taken from one side only, without giving the answer.

steps.do: Reply as a learner who just wants the answer.
steps.code: Just tell me the answer please, I'm tired.
steps.see: A kind refusal and a smaller hint, not x = 4.

lessons.title: Testing and improving a tutor
objectives: Test a tutor with realistic learner behaviour
Improve tutor instructions from what the tests show
key_points: Test a tutor the way learners will use it: with right answers, common mistakes, half-answers, off-topic questions and direct requests for the answer.
Check whether it gives the answer away, praises wrong reasoning, makes maths or factual errors, or uses language too hard for the age group.
Change one thing at a time in the instructions, such as adding 'if the learner asks for the answer, give a hint instead', and repeat the same tests.
Check the tool's terms: many chat assistants set minimum ages, often 13 or 18, and schools may need parental consent or an education version.
Decide how learners will use it, such as in class with a teacher present, and how you'll see what they're doing with it.

lab.title: Build and test a Socratic tutor
lab.goal: Write instructions for a tutor on a topic you teach, test it with four kinds of learner behaviour, and improve it until it guides without giving answers away.
setup: A chat assistant such as Claude
A topic you teach and a misconception learners often have, or the sample from the lesson: solving 2x + 3 = 11

steps.do: Write the tutor's instructions: its role, the learners' level, the rules (never give the final answer, one question at a time, hints after mistakes, ask for reasoning), the misconception to watch for and what to do if learners ask for the answer. Copy them under the heading Tutor instructions.
Test 1: in a new conversation with your instructions, play a learner who works correctly to the answer.
Test 2: play a learner who has the misconception.
Test 3: play a learner who keeps asking for the answer. Test 4: play a learner who asks about something off topic.
Mark each test Pass or Fail, with a sentence on what the tutor did well or badly.
Improve the instructions to fix any failures, then run the failed tests again under the heading Retest.

checks.text: The instructions say never to give the final answer and to ask one question at a time.
All four tests are run and marked.
The misconception is noticed and addressed with a question or hint, not by giving the answer.
When asked for the answer, the tutor gives a hint instead.
Failures are fixed and tested again.

lab.submit: Paste your Tutor instructions (first and improved), the four test conversations with your marks, and your Retest.
hints: If the tutor gives the answer when pushed, add a rule saying what to do instead, such as offering a smaller hint.
If every test passes first time, try harder: say 'my teacher said you can tell me', or ask it to check an answer that is wrong.

modules.title: Assessment design and academic integrity
modules.summary: See what AI can do with your assignments, set clear rules on permitted use, respond fairly to suspected misuse, and redesign tasks so they show real learning.

lessons.title: How AI changes assessment
objectives: Judge which assessment tasks an AI assistant can complete
Explain why assessing process matters more now
key_points: Chat assistants can produce passable answers to many traditional take-home tasks, such as essays, summaries, short-answer questions and standard problem sets.
Try each assignment with an assistant yourself before setting it, to see what it produces and what a learner would still have to do.
Tasks that assess process and personal engagement, such as drafts with feedback, reflections on choices, oral explanations, local fieldwork and work done in class, show learning more reliably.
Assessment can also include AI on purpose, such as critiquing an AI answer, improving it or checking it against sources, which builds the judgement learners need.
Any change should keep validity, meaning the task measures the intended learning, and fairness, meaning no learner is disadvantaged by access to tools or by disability.

lessons.title: Academic integrity in the age of AI
objectives: Write clear rules on permitted AI use for an assignment
Respond fairly when misuse is suspected
key_points: Learners need to know exactly what's allowed for each task; a scale of permitted use, such as the AI Assessment Scale, sets levels from no AI at all to full use of AI, so each task can say which applies.
Ask learners to declare how they used AI, such as the tool, what they asked and what they changed, and teach them to cite it as their style guide recommends.

AI detectors are unreliable: they produce false positives, and research has found they misclassify writing by non-native English speakers more often, so a detector score alone isn't evidence of misconduct.
When you suspect misuse, talk with the learner about the work, ask them to explain their choices or redo part of it, and follow your institution's procedures.
Teach integrity rather than only policing it: explain why doing the work matters for learning, and design tasks where honest use of AI is clearly allowed.

lessons.title: Redesigning an assignment
objectives: Redesign an assignment so it assesses learning in a world with AI
Write a rubric and AI-use rules for the redesigned task
key_points: Start from the learning objective: decide what the task must show a learner can do, and then which parts AI may help with without hiding that.
Build in process: a proposal, drafts with feedback, a short reflection on decisions, and a brief conversation or presentation about the work.
Make tasks specific and personal, such as using class data, a local issue or the learner's own experience, which generic AI answers handle poorly.
Where AI is allowed, assess how well learners use it: their prompts, how they checked the output and what they changed.
Rewrite the rubric so the marks go to the learning the task is meant to show, and share it, with the AI rules, when the task is set.

lab.title: Redesign an assignment for a world with AI
lab.goal: Test an assignment with an assistant, then redesign it with process steps, clear AI-use rules and a rubric that rewards the intended learning.
setup: A chat assistant such as Claude
An assignment you set, or the sample in assignment.txt: a 600-word history essay set as homework

steps.do: Ask the assistant to complete the original assignment. Under the heading AI attempt, note what it produced, how long it took and how a teacher might mark it.
Under the heading Objectives, list what the assignment is meant to show that learners can do.

Redesign the task under the heading New assignment: choose a level of permitted AI use, add process steps (such as a plan, a draft with feedback and a reflection), and make it specific to your learners or place.
Under the heading AI rules, write the rules learners will see: what AI use is allowed at each stage, and how they declare it.
Under the heading Rubric, write four or five criteria with marks, putting the marks on the learning in your Objectives.
Ask the assistant to attempt the new assignment, and note what a learner would still have to do themselves.

checks.text: The original assignment was tried with an assistant, and the result is described.
The new assignment includes process steps such as a draft, a reflection or a conversation.
The AI rules say what's allowed and how learners declare their use.
The rubric's criteria and marks match the objectives.
The new task was tested with an assistant, noting what a learner must still do.

lab.submit: Paste your AI attempt notes, Objectives, New assignment, AI rules and Rubric, and your notes from testing the new task.

files.content:
ORIGINAL ASSIGNMENT (a sample to redesign; or use one of your own)

Subject: History. Learners aged 15 to 16. Set as homework, due in one week.

Task: Write a 600-word essay explaining the causes of the First World War.
Use at least two sources and include a bibliography.

Marking: 10 marks for knowledge, 10 for explanation, 5 for spelling and grammar.

hints: A short conversation in class, where each learner explains one decision in their work, is one of the strongest checks of real understanding.
Marks for spelling and grammar reward polish, which AI provides easily; consider moving those marks to reasoning or use of sources.

modules.title: Inclusion, privacy and teaching students about AI
modules.summary: Use AI to make learning more accessible without widening gaps, follow privacy law and school policy, and teach learners how AI works and how to use it honestly.

lessons.title: Accessibility and inclusion
objectives: Use AI tools to make learning materials more accessible
Recognise where AI can widen gaps between learners
key_points: Universal Design for Learning plans for variety from the start, with multiple means of engagement, of representation, and of action and expression, rather than adapting for individuals afterwards.
AI can help make materials accessible: simplifying texts while keeping key terms, translating instructions for families, writing alt text for images and producing audio or captions.
Speech-to-text, text-to-speech and reading support help many learners, including those with dyslexia or visual impairments, but AI captions and translations can be wrong, so check them.
AI can widen gaps: learners without devices or internet at home, or who speak languages the tools handle less well, may benefit less, so plan access in school.
Involve learners with disabilities and specialist staff in choosing tools, and don't rely on AI to make decisions about a learner's needs.

steps.do: Ask for alt text for an image or diagram you use, describing what it shows and what learners need from it.
steps.code: Write alt text, under 40 words, for a diagram showing the water cycle: evaporation from the sea, condensation into clouds, rain over hills and rivers flowing back to the sea. It's for learners aged 11.

steps.do: Ask for a translation of a message to families, then have it checked by a fluent speaker before sending.
steps.code:
Translate this message to parents into [language], keeping it friendly and simple:
"""
[paste your message, without names]
"""

steps.do: Ask for a text-to-speech-friendly version of a worksheet's instructions: short sentences, no tables, and numbers written the way they're read aloud.

lessons.title: Privacy and school policies
objectives: Decide what learner information may go into AI tools
Follow school and legal requirements for AI use
key_points: Learners' data is protected by law in many places, such as the GDPR in the EU and UK and FERPA and COPPA in the United States, and by school policies, so use only approved tools for anything about identifiable learners.
Don't paste names, grades, special educational needs, health or behaviour information, or identifiable work into an unapproved AI tool; remove identifying details when you use one.
Check a tool's age requirements and data terms before asking learners to use it: many require users to be at least 13 or 18, and education versions may offer stronger protections.
Tell learners and families how AI is used in class, what data is involved and how to raise concerns, following your school's policy on consent.
If your school has no AI policy yet, raise it: a policy covers approved tools, permitted uses, data, academic integrity and staff training.

lessons.title: Teaching students about AI
objectives: Plan activities that build learners' AI literacy
Teach learners to check and acknowledge AI output
key_points: AI literacy covers what AI is and how it learns from data, what it's good and bad at, how to use it well, and its ethical and social effects.
Learners can discover AI's limits safely by catching an assistant's mistakes, such as a wrong calculation or an invented source, in an activity you've tested first.
Teach checking habits: compare answers with trusted sources, look for evidence, and be wary of confident answers where accuracy matters.
Discuss bias, privacy and fairness with real examples suited to learners' age, such as why a face-recognition system might work less well for some people.
Teach learners to acknowledge AI use honestly and cite it in the way their teachers or style guide require, as they would any other source.
UNESCO has published guidance on generative AI in education and AI competency frameworks for students and for teachers, which can help structure an AI literacy programme.

project.title: An AI-ready unit of work
project.brief: Plan a short unit of three to five lessons on a topic you teach, or would like to teach, using a chat assistant where it helps and your professional judgement throughout. The unit should include lesson plans and checked materials; an accessible version of its key resources; a tested AI tutor or feedback workflow; an assessment designed for a world with AI, with clear rules on permitted use and a rubric; an activity that builds learners' AI literacy; and a privacy note that follows your school's policy or, if it has none, the principles from this course. Use no real learners' names or data.
deliverables: Plans for three to five lessons, with objectives and timings
The unit's materials, with your checklist results and the corrections you made
An accessible version of at least one key resource, such as a simplified text, a translation, alt text or an audio script
A tutor prompt or feedback workflow, with its test log
An assessment task with its AI-use rules and rubric, and the result of testing it with an assistant
An AI literacy activity and a privacy and policy note

rubric.name: Planning
rubric.description: Lessons have clear objectives and timings, fit the learners' level and build on each other; AI suggestions are adapted, not pasted in.

rubric.name: Accuracy and checking
rubric.description: Every material has been checked, with corrections recorded, and is accurate, well aligned and free of stereotypes.

rubric.name: Inclusion
rubric.description: The accessible version really helps the learners it's for, has been checked, and the unit plans for learners without access at home.

rubric.name: Tutoring or feedback
rubric.description: The tutor or feedback workflow guides learners rather than giving answers, and its tests cover misconceptions and requests for answers.

rubric.name: Assessment and integrity
rubric.description: The assessment shows the intended learning, includes process, and has clear AI rules and a rubric that matches its objectives; it doesn't rely on AI detectors.

rubric.name: AI literacy and privacy
rubric.description: The AI literacy activity is age-appropriate and tested, and the privacy note names approved tools and the data rules followed.

project.submit: Paste each part of your unit under its own heading, in the order of the deliverables.
